sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain any two features of the Permanent Settlement.
questions.answer: (1) Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793 in Bengal and Bihar, it made zamindars hereditary owners of land who deposited a fixed amount of revenue in the treasury. (2) If a zamindar failed to pay on time his land was sold; the British got a fixed income and the zamindars became their political allies.

questions.q: Why did the British invest in improving transport in India? Give two reasons.
questions.answer: (1) Railways connected the raw-material-producing areas with the ports so cotton, indigo and other crops could be exported easily. (2) They carried British finished goods to markets all over India; British investors also got a guaranteed 5% profit on railway capital.

or.q: Why did the British create a class of English-educated Indians? Give two reasons.
or.answer: (1) English-educated Indians could work as clerks on low wages, reducing the cost of administration. (2) The British hoped this class would be loyal, appreciate British culture, spread it to others and increase the market for British goods, strengthening British rule.

questions.q: Explain any two reasons why the class of moneylenders grew during British rule.
questions.answer: (1) The time-bound and excessive revenue demands forced peasants to borrow from moneylenders. (2) The new legal system helped moneylenders, who charged high interest and used false accounts; when peasants could not repay, their land passed to them.

questions.q: Why did the British pressurise Indian farmers to cultivate indigo?
questions.answer: Indigo was needed in England as a dye for cloth produced in British mills. Farmers were forced to grow it on 3/20th of their land and sell it on terms dictated by British planters.

questions.q: Mention two legal measures which helped improve the status of women in British India.
questions.answer: (1) Sati was banned in 1829 by Lord Bentinck. (2) The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 allowed widows to remarry. (The Sharda Act of 1929 also prevented child marriage.)

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: How did the British use political power, trade policies and education to strengthen their control over India? Analyse.
questions.answer: (1) Political power: through wars (Plassey, Buxar), the Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Lapse they annexed Indian states and ruled directly. (2) Trade policies: they monopolised trade, bought raw materials cheap, let British goods in duty-free and taxed Indian goods, ruining Indian industry and making India a supplier of raw materials and a market. (3) Education: English education produced cheap, loyal clerks and a class that admired British culture and helped run the administration.

questions.q: Explain the impact of British trade on the Indian handloom weaving industry.
questions.answer: British machine-made cloth was cheap and entered India without duty, while Indian handicrafts were taxed heavily and Britain put protective tariffs on Indian textiles. India changed from an exporter of cloth to an exporter of raw cotton and importer of British cloth. Handloom weaving collapsed (de-industrialisation), weavers became unemployed and moved to villages as farm labourers, increasing pressure on agriculture.

questions.q: Why did the British pressurise the cultivation of indigo in India? Explain the reasons for the discontent of the farmers.
questions.answer: Indigo was needed as a dye for British textile mills. Discontent: (1) farmers were forced to grow indigo on 3/20th of their land; (2) they had to sell it at prices dictated by the planters; (3) indigo cultivation made the land infertile for some years and reduced land for food crops.

questions.q: Explain the impact of the British education policy on India.
questions.answer: (1) English was introduced to create cheap clerks and a loyal class; the Charter Act of 1813 and Wood's Despatch (1854) led to English schools and universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (1857). (2) Mass and elementary education was neglected; education became a monopoly of the rich and city dwellers. (3) But English became a link language and Western ideas of liberty, equality and democracy spread, producing reformers and nationalists.

questions.q: Distinguish between the Permanent Settlement and the Mahalwari Settlement.
questions.answer: Permanent Settlement (1793, Bengal and Bihar): the zamindar was made the hereditary owner and paid a fixed revenue; his land was sold if he failed to pay. Mahalwari Settlement (1822, North-Western Provinces, Punjab, Ganga valley): revenue was assessed on the produce of a mahal (village or group of villages) and all its proprietors were jointly responsible. Under both, revenue demands were very high and peasants suffered.

questions.q: Why did the British seek to restrict the development of India? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) Britain wanted India as a source of cheap raw materials for its factories. (2) It wanted India as a market for its finished goods, so Indian industries were not allowed to compete. (3) Heavy duties on Indian goods and free entry for British goods protected British industry. These policies drained India's wealth and kept it poor.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the economic impact of British rule on India in six points.
questions.answer: (1) De-industrialisation: cheap, duty-free British cloth ruined Indian handlooms and other crafts. (2) India became an exporter of raw materials and importer of finished goods. (3) The Permanent, Mahalwari and Ryotwari settlements imposed very high land revenue, impoverishing peasants. (4) Commercialisation of agriculture (indigo, opium, cotton, tea) reduced food crops and led to famines. (5) Peasants fell into debt and lost land to moneylenders; a new middle class of agents and zamindars arose. (6) There was an enormous drain of wealth to Britain through profits, salaries and pensions; railways were built mainly to serve British trade.

questions.q: Highlight the impact of the British on Indian society and culture in the 19th century.
questions.answer: (1) Western ideas of liberty, equality and human rights reached India and inspired reformers like Raja Ram Mohan Roy. (2) Laws were passed against sati (1829), for widow remarriage (1856), inter-caste marriage (1872) and against child marriage (Sharda Act 1929). (3) English education created a new middle class and a link language. (4) Orientalists founded the Asiatic Society and Fort William College, reviving interest in India's past. (5) The press, literature and theatre spread national consciousness. (6) But Indians were excluded from high posts, justice was costly and discriminatory, and the Divide and Rule policy harmed Hindu–Muslim relations.
